cards.title: Separate New vs Existing Customer Ad Spend
cards.summary: Segment paid media reporting by new and returning customers so you can see whether spend is buying growth or just harvesting people who would buy anyway.
cards.use_when: Auditing or restructuring paid acquisition for your store when topline revenue has plateaued despite a reported 'healthy' ROAS.
steps: Split your ad account reporting so new-customer and existing-customer spend and revenue are tracked separately, not blended into one campaign total. In the source's audits, many brands never delineate between the two at all.

Index your key metrics against new-customer revenue rather than total revenue, because returning-customer revenue is largely a function of your product, model and industry, not incremental ad performance.

Pull frequency on existing customers — how many times existing customers see your ads every 30 days. The presenter says he pulls this in every audit and commonly sees 20 to 100; something around 10 is offered as an informal, not universal, target.

If existing-customer frequency is very high, treat pulling that budget as a candidate test rather than an automatic win — the source notes 10 to 20 frequency may occasionally still be incremental, but usually is not.
Confirm the change with a platform conversion-lift (geo-holdout) experiment on the existing-customer campaign rather than trusting reported ROAS.
caveats: Frequency bands (10, 20-100) are the presenter's rule-of-thumb from audits, not an established benchmark.
Conversion-lift experiments are platform features; verify current availability and setup in your ad platform's interface.
A nine-figure CPG brand reportedly showed negligible incrementality on existing-customer spend, but this is one example, not a guarantee for your store.

cards.title: Why ROAS Is a Flawed Primary KPI
cards.summary: ROAS fails as a north-star metric because it is last-click, easily skewed by existing customers, and drives budget misallocation toward bottom-of-funnel.
cards.use_when: Choosing which marketing KPI to report to leadership or to optimize daily spend against for your store.
steps: Recognize three structural limits of ROAS: it can be skewed by existing customers, it reflects the last click rather than what created awareness, and it is distorted by whatever attribution settings are in use.

Note that branded search and retargeting campaigns naturally show high ROAS because they capture high-intent traffic that would likely have converted anyway, while genuinely awareness-building activity (the source's example is TV) has a return that is unmeasurable at that layer.

Test any metric against the source's rule: if a metric does not hold up across every context, it is probably flawed. The presenters argue incrementality, net profit, new-customer acquisition cost and CLTV survive context changes, while ROAS does not.

Where you still use ROAS, treat it as directional context, and note that some large-brand performance operators aim for the lowest ROAS at which they can acquire customers profitably rather than maximizing ROAS.
For large or multi-channel operations, be aware that ROAS has been reported up to executives for a long time, so repositioning the KPI may be slow and political.
caveats: The claim that ROAS should never be a primary KPI is the presenters' strong opinion, not a universal rule.
The claim that top US operators 'optimize for lowest ROAS possible' is the speaker's observation of an unnamed cohort, not a documented benchmark.
Attribution and platform metric behavior changes; verify current platform reporting before acting.

cards.title: Split Klaviyo Attributed Revenue by New vs Returning
cards.summary: Klaviyo-attributed revenue is a useful north-star but is inflated by default view-through-style settings and should be split by customer type.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing your email/SMS retention KPIs and deciding whether to optimize campaigns for attributed revenue.
steps: Understand what Klaviyo's default attribution captures: the source describes it as 5-day open, 5-day click and says the open component functions essentially as a view-through metric that credits emails for purchases high-intent customers were going to make anyway.
Use attributed revenue as a directional north star: if it is rising, you are probably reaching converting people — but do not treat it as the definitive measure of retention success.
Split attributed revenue between new and returning customers. The source argues Klaviyo's impact on a new customer is far less incremental than on a returning customer.

Do not chase revenue-per-campaign as a primary KPI. Optimizing for it drives aggressive cadence — touching as many people as possible before they buy — which the presenters say can damage brand and customer attention.

Benchmark against the Klaviyo default settings if useful, since most users run them, but treat reported increments as needing conversion-lift or incrementality validation before you make budget calls.
caveats: Default attribution windows are platform behavior that can change; verify current Klaviyo attribution settings and options in the interface.

The source is critiquing an ad claim that '50% of revenue from Klaviyo' is a benchmark; the presenters call this meaningless as a guarantee and say the figure depends on business model (furniture vs supplements).
Incrementality of email to new vs returning customers is described as nuanced and ultimately needs testing, not assumption.

cards.title: Convert Classroom or Lecture Attacks into Storefront Defensive Controls
cards.summary: Turn any demonstrated attack scenario into the vulnerability condition it reveals, then apply concrete controls and validate only on systems you own.
cards.use_when: Reviewing security of your storefront, checkout, customer accounts, admin panels, integrations or ecommerce automation, and turning a demonstration into prevention.
steps: Restate the attack as a defensive condition rather than a procedure: identify what an attacker needs (a missing authorization check, an unvalidated input, an over-scoped token, an exposed secret) and which asset it exposes.

Apply the matching control: enforce authentication and authorization separately and explicitly on every endpoint, encrypt sensitive data in transit and at rest, hash stored credentials with a proper password-hashing scheme, and sign tokens/messages where integrity matters.

Keep authentication (who you are), authorization (what you may do), encryption (confidentiality in transit/at rest), hashing (one-way credential storage) and signing (tamper-evidence) as distinct concerns and check each is present where required.
Scope any agent or integration access to the specific brand and task; treat retrieved documents, web content and tool output as untrusted data, never as authorization for an action.
Validate only on systems you own or have written permission to test, using non-destructive checks; do not capture credentials or reuse live secrets.
Log authentication, authorization decisions and agent tool calls so you can detect and reconstruct misuse.
caveats: No single control is sufficient: HTTPS, hashing, CAPTCHA, a WAF or prompt filtering alone do not guarantee security.
Browser behavior, configuration options, algorithms and vendor claims change over time; verify current settings and defaults rather than treating any historical detail as universal.
Legal and policy requirements around security vary by jurisdiction and platform; confirm your obligations rather than assuming.

cards.title: Frequency Audit as a First Step to Cutting Existing-Customer Waste
cards.summary: A simple frequency check in the ad account reveals how heavily you are re-targeting buyers and gives an intuitive basis for pulling budget.
cards.use_when: Preparing an audit or budget-review of your store's paid media, especially existing-customer targeting.
steps: Pull the frequency metric for existing-customer audiences over the last 30 days in your ad platform.
Compare against a rough sense of what is reasonable: the presenter offers around 10 exposures per 30 days as a plausible point of reference, while noting most audits he sees run 20 to 100.

If frequency is far above that, treat the excess budget as a candidate for reallocation, but frame it as a hypothesis — the source explicitly says moving from 10 to 20 may occasionally be incremental.
Where you can, follow up with a platform conversion-lift or geo-holdout experiment on that campaign to measure actual incremental contribution rather than relying on frequency alone.

Segment repeat buyers who have gone quiet on owned channels (e.g. purchased and unsubscribed) as the limited case where paid re-acquisition of existing customers may be reasonable — the source notes it is 'something smart to do' versus blindly targeting all existing customers.
caveats: Frequency thresholds are the speaker's heuristics from audits, not documented benchmarks.
Even a careful re-acquisition test on existing customers reportedly did nothing in the source's example; treat any spend there as experimental.
Conversion-lift experiment features, setup and reporting windows vary by platform; verify current interface.

cards.title: Match Ad Spend Allocation to Your Repurchase Cycle
cards.summary: How much to spend re-targeting existing customers depends on how often your product can realistically be repurchased.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget split between acquisition and existing/retention-oriented paid media for your specific product category.
steps: Estimate your category's natural repurchase cycle. The source contrasts high-ticket furniture (repurchased roughly once every five years, per the presenter) with fast-moving consumables that generate frequent returns.
For long repurchase cycles, expect poor cohort lift and avoid spending heavily on paid ads to people who have already bought.

For fast-moving consumables with high likelihood of returns, a small amount of spend on specific segments may be justified — the source's example is people who purchased and unsubscribed, whom direct channels can no longer reach.
Rather than blanket-targeting existing customers, define narrow segments (unsubscribed buyers, lapsed repeat cohorts) where owned channels cannot reach them.
Validate any such spend with an incrementality or conversion-lift test before scaling, since even smart-looking segments may test as non-incremental.
caveats: The furniture and consumable examples are illustrative; confirm your own cohort data rather than assuming a category norm.
The source does not give a numeric budget split; treat any allocation as a business-specific judgment.

cards.title: Treat Awareness-Funnel Spend Cautiously but Recognize It Drives Sales
cards.summary: Top-of-funnel activity can be genuinely valuable yet unmeasurable in last-click systems, so it gets under-funded relative to retargeting.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget across the funnel and interpreting reports that show strong branded/retargeting ROAS versus weak upper-funnel numbers.
steps: Recognize that last-click attribution will credit branded search and retargeting for conversions influenced by earlier awareness activity, making upper-funnel spend look bad.
Expect that if you only fund what reports well, you will systematically overallocate to bottom-of-funnel and to existing customers.
Use an alternative like incrementality testing or geo-holdouts where possible to estimate the upper-funnel contribution that platform reporting hides.

Accept that some awareness channels (the source cites TV) may not have a directly measurable return at that layer, only a downstream effect — reflect this in how you judge them rather than writing them off.
When you can't measure directly, treat the decision as a judgment call and keep the spend bounded and reviewable rather than either ignoring it or scaling it blindly.
caveats: This is a structural limitation of attribution systems, not a license to spend without any measurement.
Incrementality testing methods vary in rigor and availability; use the strongest option your platform and budget allow.

cards.title: Measure Retention by Fundamentals, Not Email KPIs
cards.summary: Retention is primarily driven by product, portfolio, customer experience and pricing; email and owned media amplify, they rarely fix, weak retention.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing poor repeat purchase rates before investing in more email flows, upsells or cross-sells.
steps: First establish your baseline: check whether a meaningful portion of customers return on their own without marketing intervention. The source says you should; if you don't, extra marketing will not create it.

Walk the retention drivers the source lists — product quality, product portfolio, repeatability, customer experience, competitive landscape, pricing and the broader economy — and treat them as the upstream causes.
Use email and owned media to amplify those fundamentals: the source notes good brands use email to foster community, build loyalty and VIP programs, and run abandonment sequences.

In flows, prioritize communicating things that affect the customer experience — the source's example is that complex or instruction-dependent products should be explained rather than immediately pushed toward an upsell or cross-sell.
Treat Klaviyo (or any ESP) as a channel that can improve or worsen experience, but not as the fix for deep retention problems.
caveats: This is the presenters' strong opinion ('retention is not a flows problem, most of the time') and is framed against common agency pitches — it is a prioritization argument, not a claim that flows are unimportant.
The five-driver list is a conversational enumeration, not a formal framework.

cards.title: Tie Spend Scaling to Net Profit, Not Absolute Budget
cards.summary: Scaling is not the same as increasing spend; the source reframes the goal as profitable growth rather than revenue at any cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise ad budgets, or evaluating advice that tells you to simply spend more on Meta.
steps: Question the assumption that a higher budget equals a bigger business. The source's counter is that anyone can increase spend without making more money.

Assess scaling against profit-focused metrics (net profit, CLTV, cash flow) rather than revenue or ROAS alone. The presenters note the industry narrative moved toward profit and cash-flow focus after the 2020-era growth-at-all-costs period.

If you do raise budget, watch revenue returns tightly and be ready to pull back. The source acknowledges that in the earlier era, a simple meaningful budget bump plus a few weeks sometimes produced more revenue — but that this is not reliable now.

Be aware that reported metrics from different channels (e.g. a much higher attributed number from email than from Meta) can mislead executive or owner decisions about where to add resources; treat channel-reported returns skeptically.
Where you are a young or small business, prioritize not going broke over matching competitors' spend levels.
caveats: The source gives no numeric profit benchmark of its own; a reference to a 20% net profit figure is attributed to another commentator, not presented as a universal rule.
The earlier-era advice to 'just increase budget' is described as having worked in a specific time window; it is not a current recommendation.

cards.title: Score Metrics by Whether They Hold Up in Any Context
cards.summary: A practical filter for choosing KPIs: prefer metrics that remain meaningful no matter the business model, time frame or channel.
cards.use_when: Selecting which metrics to hold as your north star and which to demote to context-only when managing your store's performance.
steps: List your current KPIs and, for each, ask whether it would still make sense across different business models, time windows and channels.
Keep as top-level metrics the ones that survive that test. The source names incrementality, net profit, customer lifetime value and new-customer acquisition cost as examples.
Demote context-dependent metrics — the source names ROAS and Klaviyo attributed revenue — to supporting indicators, since they can break or fail to influence net profit in some contexts.
When a context-dependent metric moves sharply, investigate before reacting, especially if the movement coincides with channel-reported returns that may not be incremental.
Revisit the list periodically, since platform reporting and attribution behavior change and can reintroduce context-dependence.
caveats: This is the speaker's personal framework, presented as a heuristic, not an established measurement standard.
Even the surviving metrics require correct calculation and clean data; the source does not specify formulas.

cards.title: Debug a Reported ROAS That Doesn't Match Topline
cards.summary: When reported ROAS stays healthy but revenue is flat, the likely cause is that spend is harvesting existing or high-intent buyers rather than acquiring new ones.
cards.use_when: Investigating a store where the ad account reports a 'healthy' ROAS (e.g. 4-5x) but total revenue has plateaued for months.
steps: Compare reported ROAS against topline revenue trend over the same period. If ROAS is 'fine' but revenue has not moved or is flat year on year, the metric and the business are telling different stories.
Check whether new and existing customer spend are separated at all — the presenters say many brands don't segment this, which hides the problem.
Look for spend concentrated on existing customers, high-intent organic audiences, and retargeting, which produces short-term high ROAS that eventually dries up as the pool is exhausted.

Note that a growing audience of followers or subscribers who have not purchased can look like incremental opportunity but is really high-intent traffic you already own being pushed through the funnel, which dries up too.
Set new-customer revenue (not total revenue) as the framing metric to reveal the underlying acquisition trend.
caveats: The 4-5x ROAS figure is a client example cited in the source, not a benchmark for good or bad performance.
The pattern described is a diagnostic hypothesis; confirm with segmentation and, ideally, incrementality testing.
